# Project Call Relationships: Code-Reading Notes

This time I reorganized the notes by going back through the file itself. `lib/xcodeproj/project.rb` has more than just an "open project" entry point: construction of `Project`, opening by path, initialization branches, and text output all appear here. When reading a caller, first note which method it enters, then continue tracing the object's state.

```text
lib/xcodeproj/project.rb
  |
  +-- Project (42)
      +-- initialize(path, skip_initialization = false) (58)
      +-- self.open(path) (88)
      +-- to_s (129)
      +-- initialize_from_scratch (147)
      +-- initialize_from_file (171)
      `-- new_from_plist (225)
```

`class Project` on line 42 is the starting reference for this page. For `initialize(path, skip_initialization = false)` on line 58, record both the path and the second argument. A caller that omits the second argument needs a different reading focus from one that explicitly passes an argument to skip initialization; copying only `Project.new` loses that branch information. Don't interpret the parameter name as the call's outcome here; follow the method body to determine the outcome.

`self.open(path)` on line 88 is a class-method entry point. Both it and instance initialization accept a path, but that alone doesn't establish their relationship. When tracing back, follow the usage into `self.open(path)` and record the returned object alongside the next step in the method body; for calls that construct an object directly, return to line 58 to compare. This keeps the records for "entering from an existing path" and "getting an object first, then processing it" from merging into a single trace.

`to_s` on line 129 is on the output side. If a caller uses it in logging, debugging, or error display, first record it as a string output point. Converting a Project object to text is no substitute for reading how it was first created or opened; opening by path, blank initialization, and plist-related entry points still need to be traced back individually. This location sits in the middle of the entry-point index because it often comes into view while reading call results, but it isn't the same kind of operation as an initialization method.

The last three locations are the ones that need to be checked side by side. First compare `initialize_from_scratch` on line 147 with new-project scenarios; place `initialize_from_file` on line 171 alongside calls related to paths and files; trace `new_from_plist` on line 225 on its own. Method names give a direction for the search. The name alone doesn't justify classifying `new_from_plist` as file initialization, nor should the three locations' order in the source be treated as a single execution sequence. These notes don't record the findings on calls between them, so that gap remains here.

The code-reading order I'm using is now:

1. Distinguish `Project.new` from `Project.open` at the call site;
2. For direct construction, note the state of the arguments passed to `path` and `skip_initialization`;
3. Return to lines 147, 171, and 225, and follow the method bodies to confirm which initialization branches are actually reached;
4. Finally, check the uses of `to_s` on line 129, and record the purpose of the text it produces independently.

The line numbers aren't decorative: line 42 defines the object's scope, lines 58 and 88 mark the two entry points, line 129 corresponds to output, and lines 147, 171, and 225 are candidate initialization destinations. For the adjacent PlainInformative notes, see DOC-02; that is only navigation for adjacent calls. Reading Project itself still starts with this file.

Still missing are the specific call relationships among the three initialization methods and the branch each caller ultimately reaches. If call snippets corresponding to the method bodies become available next time, append them directly to this index; the entry-point locations don't need to change.

# PlainInformative Reading Adjacent Code

This note is kept under `lib/xcodeproj.rb` because the search results for PlainInformative easily jumble together the names near the entry point. The first time I got here, scrolling down through adjacent locations was the fastest approach; only when I came back later did I realize that this approach treated "names appearing in the same section" and "a direct call exists between the names" as the same thing.

The entry file is still a suitable starting point. It shows where PlainInformative first appears and preserves the neighboring names encountered during that reading; the entry itself does not fill in an object-level explanation for those names. The main value of the old record is to bring the reader back to the same location, not to make a judgment about the object relationships that follow.

The marks in the margin at the time can be organized as follows:

```text
lib/xcodeproj.rb
  Names near PlainInformative
  └─ Check calls in the same section
     └─ Check the Project side separately
```

These lines show the reading order, not a call graph. The first-level arrow does not indicate an object ownership relationship, and the second level does not mean that Project is created by the preceding item. Reading this little diagram as a relationship graph earlier made the organization at the entry point look more specific than it actually was.

## Outdated Sequential Reading Method

The initial draft used a loose assumption: as long as PlainInformative and the other names appeared in the same section, continue tracing along the same line. The benefit was that there was no need to stop at the entry point to sort things out, and Project could be added immediately to the same margin list when encountered.

The problem was that the purpose of the list changed. It was originally meant only to indicate "where to look next," but was later used to answer "whose direct adjacent call this is." The two questions require different evidence. The former needs only the entry location; the latter requires at least returning to the actual call near the name and cannot be replaced by appearing in the same section.

Therefore, the old draft's statement that "following names in the same section will find the actual relationship" no longer applies, but is still retained here. Someone may find this page using the old search terms; deleting it would instead remove the rationale for the old reading method. The original approach can still be used as a shortcut for browsing files, but it cannot be used to place all neighboring names on the same level.

## Stop Points When Revisiting

After review, the content beside the entry was split by reading action rather than stacked by name:

- When `lib/xcodeproj.rb` shows PlainInformative, first note the calls visible immediately adjacent to it. This record covers only this small span of adjacency and does not extend to the behavior of subsequent objects.
- If the next question has become what the Project object does, stop at the entry point. Continuing to add inferences to this page at that point would mix the two object levels together again.
- When returning to the original location, add a note only when a directly connected call is seen again; an occurrence with the same name but no adjacency is still read at its own location.

This does not turn the entry file into a master index. Instead, it gives the entry one local responsibility: providing the first location and a short, visible adjacent relationship. The PlainInformative side is suitable for answering where to start reading, not for providing a complete explanation of Project.

## Separation from the Project Record

The DOC-03 record was later added as a parallel record of Project's adjacent calls. The two pages can link to each other, but should not be merged into a name list: this page stops near the `lib/xcodeproj.rb` entry, while the reading path for DOC-03 unfolds from the Project side. Writing Project into this page does not automatically make it a direct neighbor of PlainInformative.

This distinction also explains why the old note seems somewhat contradictory. One part records the names seen in the entry section, while the other requires opening the object context further to explain them; they are adjacent in the original margin notes, but are not the same kind of fact. When rereading, retaining the former first and then deciding whether to switch to DOC-03 helps avoid mistaking search order for a call relationship.

## Remaining Margin Notes

The old notes do not retain enough detail to determine whether annotation names near the entry should be color-coded separately from executable calls. At this point, keep only the practice of recording them separately first; do not turn it into a fixed tagging rule.

Another easy-to-misread point is that the name for PlainInformative appearing on the entry side does not mean that all subsequent reading must return here. The entry keeps the thread anchored; once the question has moved to the Project side, continue from its actual occurrence there.

# Project Call Path Guide

`lib/xcodeproj/project/object_attributes.rb` is still the entry point retained on this page. It is located in the project directory and is part of an existing Ruby module. When an old issue leads someone here, the goal usually isn't to get a complete map of Project right away, but to first map the vague phrase "property relationships" to local objects in the file.

The original diagram was not replaced; a reading guide was added beside it:

```text
Project
  └─ project/object_attributes.rb
       ├─ Property-related reading
       └─ Historical behavior check
```

## What the diagram originally referred to

Project at the top was the umbrella term used in the search at the time. Some people came from the project object, some from a property name, and others from changes after a write; the notes collapsed these entry points into one word. It reads smoothly, but layers relationships from different levels on top of one another. The first arrow in the diagram is therefore only the reading landing point within the directory; it does not mean that every runtime path passes through this file.

"Property-related reading" is the line in the old draft most likely to be misunderstood. It did not refer to any particular field, and it did not distinguish between declarations in the file, local access, and subsequent object changes. It was written that way so that investigators could first find a stable location. Treating it as a data model or as the boundary of property reads and writes would add meaning that this file never took on.

The second line, "Historical behavior check," was kept broader. It means comparing the old wording against the code while reading: sometimes the issue is simply that names are similar; sometimes the object relationship only becomes apparent elsewhere. The value of the old page is not to decide among these cases, but to let later readers return to the same file instead of starting the search over from the entire Project.

## Markers used when reading from the entry point

After review, the margin notation was changed to leave a trace of what was observed, rather than characterize the entire Project first.

- Objects or declarations that appear in the file are written under "seen." This only indicates that the reading has reached that location.
- When a name is followed from the file to another location, it is written as "continue." The arrow belongs to that reading session and is not backfilled into the old diagram.
- When an issue only becomes apparent in the write result, it is written as "result." The result may be related to the file entry point, but the result should not be turned around and described as the file's entire responsibility.

These markers initially look somewhat repetitive, but they correct a conflation in the old draft: directory location, object relationships, and call relationships had been written as a single line. Directory location answers "where to open first"; object relationships answer "what is being inspected"; call relationships require following the specific object. Once the three are separated, the old diagram remains usable, but its purpose is narrowed to navigation.

One practice from that time is also retained here. When dealing with a Project property issue, first confirm within `object_attributes.rb` which local relationship the issue is closest to, then decide whether to leave the file. This order is still useful for old links because they usually retain only broad terms such as Project or property and cannot directly indicate which object the reader originally stopped at.

## Notes added beside the diagram during review

The `object_attributes` in the filename can easily create the expectation that it should contain all property relationships. The original draft followed that expectation and drew the diagram as if it went directly from Project to the two items at the bottom. The diagram is kept, but its endpoints are now understood as two reading actions: one is to first locate a nearby object or declaration within the file; the other is to compare the old wording with the current reading position.

Directory ownership itself is no longer treated as proof of a call. Project at the top of the diagram only indicates that this note originally served Project-related searches; it does not assign a unique entry point for every property issue. If a particular reading reaches the same object from somewhere else, that relationship should be drawn separately in that record rather than forcibly merged into this old diagram.

To keep old links interpretable, the original judgment is reproduced below:

> All Project property calls can be found in this file.

This statement is outdated. `object_attributes.rb` is now treated as a fixed reading entry point for Project property issues, not as a convergence point for all calls. The old judgment was not deleted because it did shape how this page was used early on; readers just should not use it to infer the complete call chain in the project.

## How this is separated from the old code notes

DOC-06 records the old Project code notes. Both pages may be reached through the same Project wording, but their points of focus differ: this page retains the entry point, the old diagram, and the correction to the meaning of its arrows; the notes retain more scattered fragments from the reading process. When you need to determine why an old link points to `object_attributes.rb`, look at this page's diagram and old wording first. When you need to trace what kind of code was being read at the time, look through the notes.

This distinction was also added later. The original draft put "call relationships" and "old code snippets" in the same category of material, so users could easily use a snippet to add edges to the diagram or use the diagram to explain details in a snippet. Both materials still coexist, but neither is treated as an expanded version of the other.

## Old usage retained here

This page is useful for starting from a broad Project property issue, returning to `lib/xcodeproj/project/object_attributes.rb`, and then beginning the detailed reading. It no longer requires readers to first accept the old statement that "all [calls] can be found in this file." The two endpoints in the diagram do not provide a complete classification; they are only a reminder to distinguish, when reading object relationships, whether what you are seeing is content within the file, an object being followed further, or a result that has already appeared.

If a new local relationship is worth retaining later, add it beside the corresponding object and mark it as "seen," "continue," or "result." The old diagram can remain unchanged; it records the route that brought Project issues into this file at the time.

# XCScheme Call Relationship Code Tour

`lib/xcodeproj/scheme.rb` was once treated as a very thin object-forwarding graph: get XCScheme, retrieve an action, and finally obtain XML. This entry point is indeed useful for finding scheme actions first, but the old diagram collapsed "reading an object" and "still saving it through the scheme after changes" into one step. Later, using it to investigate issues made it easy to miss state changes.

The old diagram is retained here to show the investigation order used at the time:

```text
XCScheme
  -> scheme action
  -> build / test-related objects
  -> XML
```

In this diagram, the build action, test references, and XML output look like independent endpoints. That interpretation is no longer reliable. An action is a mutable object held by the scheme; when an action changes, checking its values is not enough. Follow the same XCScheme back to the save path as well. Presenting "serialization happens at the endpoint" as the only relationship was the most misleading part of this page.

When rechecking, no longer start with the full XML. First locate the corresponding scheme action through XCScheme, then inspect the collections attached to that action. The test portion needs to be identified separately: skipped tests are not an extra field on an ordinary testable reference, but a section of XML that changes with the test list. Environment variables are also part of the action's serialized content and cannot be inferred from the project's build configuration settings.

This does not mean every action has the same save behavior. The old notes covered only a local reading path down from `scheme.rb`, not the complete object hierarchy for each action. In particular, the shared entry point between the build action and test action had not been confirmed at the time; drawing them as parallel branches was just a convenience for reading the code, not an interface constraint.

We still trace back in the following order:

1. Locate the action being accessed through XCScheme, and confirm whether an existing object is being retrieved or a new object is being created.
2. If the change involves test items, check the test references and their skip lists first, then inspect the output nodes.
3. If the change involves environment variables, trace where the action's XML is generated to find the container; do not look for a concept with the same name in Project settings.
4. Finally, return to the scheme's save operation and confirm that the changes have not remained on a temporary object.

DOC-08 can serve as side notes for the old Project code, but they do not supplement this call relationship diagram. The old diagram is retained because it still helps readers get into `scheme.rb` quickly; it can no longer be used to conclude that action changes have become detached from XCScheme, or that all XML details are handled at the same layer.

# Reviewing Project Call Relationships

## This file is still the entry point

```text
lib/xcodeproj/project/object/helpers/groupable_helper.rb
```

This path has not changed. It places the file within four successive local scopes: `lib` is the source directory, `xcodeproj` is the project namespace, `project/object` points to Project's object layer, and `helpers` indicates that the final layer contains object helper logic. The `groupable` in the filename is only a navigation clue; it cannot, on its own, be treated as the name of a public object or method.

The early notes represented it as a very short Project entry-point diagram:

```text
Project
  |
  +-- object
       |
       +-- helpers
            |
            +-- groupable_helper.rb
```

The diagram is retained, but is now read in terms of directories and object layers, not with every line interpreted as a runtime call. This is because the most stable part of this material is the file's location and its neighboring files in the helper directory; Project's full object lifecycle is not covered here.

## Reading outward from the file

When opening the file, start with its declaration as the local anchor. If it declares a module, trace back through the places where that module is incorporated into the object layer. If the file only contains helper methods, use those methods' receivers and reference sites to establish which object relationships it supports. The directory name `project/object/helpers` can narrow the search, but cannot replace the declaration itself.

When tracing references, record these three relationships separately:

```text
helper file
  -> module declaration
     -> inclusion or extension sites
        -> objects using helper methods
```

# Workspace Layout and Deployment Target Decision Record

compat-2016.4 This round records two closely related things that should not be combined into one decision: the output format of workspace XML, and where the deployment target writer writes. The existing lookup starts at `lib/xcodeproj/workspace.rb`; what is visible here is a local entry point near the workspace object, not enough to attribute the entire project generation process to the same writer.

The initial question was whether the rewritten workspace file should first be sorted by path after the caller has added several FileReference. Sorted text looks easier to compare and might reduce line movement in commits, but there is no evidence yet to determine whether the caller already uses insertion order to express layout.

## Tentative Decision

Do not sort before output. When the writer receives an existing FileReference collection, preserve its existing order and standardize only the outer structure of XML. This is not a claim that order always has business meaning; it avoids having the writer introduce unrelated changes just to make the text look nicer.

For relative project paths, retain the workspace group path notation. Do not convert between absolute and relative paths here, or derive a new path base from the project name. We need to check the path text against an actual output later.

Record the deployment target separately. For now, only accept it on an existing build configuration: read the existing value and, if needed, write it back to the corresponding configuration. Do not infer the platform from the workspace filename, reference path, or target name, and do not establish a cross-target defaults layer here.

## Two Options

| Option | Benefits Seen at the Time | Concerns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sort FileReference before writing | Cleaner diff | Overrides the caller's insertion order |
| Preserve the original order | Smaller change | Text comparisons still depend on call order |

Choose the second option for now. If the caller needs a particular sort order, it should apply that when constructing the reference collection; the writer should not do a second pass on its behalf.

## Pending Review

We do not yet have raw workspace output, so we cannot determine whether the XML declaration, element opening lines, version attribute, and location relative to the Pods project need to be fixed line by line. It is also unconfirmed whether the deployment target writer and workspace writer share a serialization entry point. The next record should include local text excerpts before and after writing the same input, along with changes to the corresponding build configuration.

# Decision Record: Workspace Layout and Deployment Target

The earliest draft combined "making generated files easy to compare" with "letting the writer organize objects for the caller." After reviewing the object relationships around `lib/xcodeproj/workspace.rb`, these two judgments need to be separated: stable workspace text does not mean that the insertion order of FileReference can be overridden during output; the need to write the deployment target into configuration does not mean that it should participate in workspace path handling.

## Why the Old Judgment Initially Seemed Valid

When this page was first written, the sorting approach had an immediate appeal. Project files are frequently committed, and references arranged by path are easy to read; if the same set of objects appears in the same order every time, visual inspection is also easier. This led to the draft saying, "the writer first obtains the references, then sorts them by a stable key."

The problem with this statement is not that sorting itself is necessarily wrong, but that it assumes the writer can decide the order in which objects are presented. When the caller adds FileReference, whether it deliberately places a particular project reference first, and whether it has already sorted the collection during construction are all aspects of the object state before the writer runs. Sorting again during output would erase these distinctions and cause lines to move during an otherwise unrelated write.

The current correction is therefore: the writer does not reorder FileReference by path, UUID, or display name. It only writes the existing objects as workspace XML. Ease of line-by-line text comparison must not override the object order already established by the caller.

## Boundaries of the 2023 Review

Workspace format and deployment target should be reviewed separately.

On the workspace side, the concern is the outer structure of XML: the beginning of the file, how the Workspace element's version is represented, the relative order in which FileRef appears, and how relative project paths are written. What needs to be confirmed here is whether a write changes the existing layout, not how to derive a target's build settings from XML.

On the deployment target side, the concern is the existing build configuration. The writer should read and write values in the corresponding configuration; it should not rebuild unrelated configurations merely because the workspace contains a particular project reference, nor should it infer the platform or default version from path text. The direct benefit of this arrangement is that configuration changes do not get mixed into workspace comparisons; deployment target comparisons are likewise not affected by line breaks and reference order in XML.

The options listed at the time have not been removed:

| Approach | Benefit | Risk | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sort FileReference before output | Files are easy to compare | May change the caller's layout | Not adopted |
| Preserve input order and constrain only the outer structure of XML | Does not introduce additional object changes | Call order will still be reflected in the text | Adopted |
| Organize paths and configuration defaults together | Appears to reduce differences in old files | Packs multiple inferences into the writer | Not adopted |

The third option was not proven wrong; there simply was not enough object-level material to support it at the time. Path representations, configuration defaults, and target platforms each have their own sources. They cannot be handled together in a single step merely because they appear during the same project generation.

## Retained Old Passage

> Sorting before writing makes the files generated each time easier to compare; if the caller needs its own order, it can organize the objects before passing them to the writer.

**Deprecated.** This passage remains to explain why sorting was favored early on. The later decision was that the caller's insertion actions can themselves be part of observing workspace layout; the writer does not change them to make comparisons easier. If the caller explicitly sorts the collection, the output will naturally reflect that sorted collection, but this is not a compensating action by the writer.

Another old sentence was, "as long as Xcode can open it, minor line-break and ordering details do not matter." This also remains in the record, but is no longer a review conclusion. Opening successfully establishes only one outcome; it does not settle whether writing the text changed object order or relative path representation. Without the original snippets, a successful open should not be used to make overly broad claims about format boundaries.

## A Recheck That Was Not Fully Archived

For the second edit, a workspace containing a Pods project reference and a set of existing build configurations were prepared. The original intent was to compare reference order and paths before and after writing, then check whether the deployment target writer touched only the intended configuration. The complete output was not attached to this page, leaving only two narrow conclusions: do not sort inside the workspace writer; do not rewrite build configuration merely because a Pods path appears.

This recheck did not establish a platform-default policy. Whether missing configuration should remain absent, receive a caller-provided value, or follow a separate initialization path was unresolved at the time. Therefore, "the deployment target belongs to build configuration" cannot be expanded into "every target has the same default value."

## Review Addendum

A risk was raised during review: if the two similarly named writers share mutable objects, writing back the deployment target could indirectly affect workspace text. There was no call chain available, nor any direct evidence that this risk had materialized, so it remains only a review question. When differences appear, first save the workspace text and the corresponding configuration snippet separately, then determine whether the two are actually related.

The short statement retained from the meeting was: "Check layout against objects, and deployment target against configuration." It added no new defaults and did not expand the range of supported platforms; it only fixed the investigation order. First examine the state of the FileReference collection before writing, then examine XML; for configuration values, return to the corresponding build configuration.

## Still Undecided

- The exact text in which relative paths should be written still needs confirmation from actual output.
- Whether absolute paths should be normalized was not decided in this recheck.
- Deployment target behavior when build configuration is missing remains undecided.
- There is no current call-site material showing whether the two writers share mutable objects.

What this version settles, then, is the boundary rather than a complete compatibility strategy: preserve the existing order of FileReference, and review workspace format and deployment target configuration separately. If raw results from users' routine calls become available later, they should be added alongside these two branches, rather than merging them again into one "big write" decision.

# Decision Record: Workspace Layout and Deployment Targets

This record began with a small question: after the same set of project references is written out again, which lines were already determined by the caller, and which were produced by the writer itself? Later, the deployment target writer was brought within the scope of the consolidation under compat-2016.4, so both threads remained in the same decision record. They appear next to each other during a single project generation, but concern different objects: one is the layout of the workspace XML, and the other is the target version in the build configuration.

This page has not rewritten the old sections into an entirely new explanation. The initial sorting idea, a later review that was not fully archived, the narrowly scoped questions left by reviewers, and the entry point encountered again in 2025 are all retained below as they were understood at the time. Where statements conflict, follow the explicitly marked corrections.

## The Starting Point in 2023, Month 4

When this was first recorded, only `lib/xcodeproj/workspace.rb` and the nearby workspace objects could be located. Search terms focused on workspace, xml, to_s, filereference, version, and encoding. They were enough to narrow the issue down to the workspace writer area, but not enough to establish more distant call relationships or to show whether the deployment target passed through the same serialization entry point.

The working hypothesis at the time was simple: project files need to be committed and compared, so writing FileReference out in stable-key order might make the generated output easier to inspect. Paths also looked like presentation details, so it seemed they could be tidied up before writing as well. The draft included this statement:

> The writer first obtains FileReference, then sorts by a stable key; relative paths are normalized against the workspace root directory.

Neither part of this statement held up later. Sorting mistook "text that is easy to compare" for "the writer has the authority to reorder objects"; path normalization was not supported by any specific rules. At the time, these were only candidates written down to narrow the scope of the issue, not verified behavior.

In this version, deployment target had only a one-line note: the target version should be handled through the existing build configuration. There was no attempt here to infer the platform from the project filename, supply defaults based on target names, or propose collecting the values for all targets into a new table. The early record did not contain enough material to make those further decisions.

## Choices in the Initial Draft and Misjudgments Retained

There were actually two options at the outset.

| Approach | What seemed worthwhile at the time | Costs already recognized at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sort before writing FileReference | The diff looks tidy | May overwrite the ordering established by the caller |
| Preserve the existing order | Makes no additional changes to the objects | The text is still affected by call order |

The first draft chose the second option, but the rationale was incomplete. At the time, all we could say was: if the caller wants a particular order, it should establish that order before passing the objects to the writer; the writer will not perform a second reorganization. This choice does not claim that order has business meaning in every project; it simply avoids introducing changes at the output stage that did not previously exist.

Another early position was, "As long as Xcode can open it, line breaks and element order are just formatting details." This sentence was not deleted because it accurately reflects the acceptance practices at the time. **Later overturned.** Successful opening can remain an observation, but it cannot override whether the written text preserves reference order, preserves the representation of relative locations, or changes the layout originally established by the caller.

## Month 11 review: stability is not sorting

The second edit split the issue into two judgments. Text stability means that the writer's output format can be inspected; object-order stability means that the writer does not rewrite the existing ordering of FileReference on the caller's behalf. The former does not imply the latter, much less make sorting a default step.

After the review, we decided not to reorder FileReference by path, UUID, or display name. The writer is responsible for writing existing references as workspace XML; whether the caller sorts when constructing the collection is determined by the caller's own actions. This way, rewriting without modifying the objects will not produce unrelated line movements solely because of the writer's "tidying."

Paths were also separated from the sorting issue. Relative project references should retain their workspace group path representation; absolute locations must not be changed to relative locations merely to make the text look consistent, and vice versa. The early idea of "organizing by the workspace root directory" did not provide actionable boundaries, so it was no longer used.

The options table produced by this review is retained below:

| Option | Advantages | Costs | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sort references before output | Makes the text easier to compare line by line each time | Erases insertion order and may create unrelated diffs | Abandoned |
| Preserve input order and constrain only the outer format | Makes the layout established by the caller visible | The text will reflect call order | Adopted |
| Recalculate paths and target defaults | Seems likely to reduce differences from old files | Mixes path inference and configuration inference into the writer | Not adopted |

The third option was not proven wrong; at the time, there were simply no object relationships to support it. Relative workspace locations, target configuration keys, and platform defaults come from different layers. Even if they are processed sequentially during the same generation run, they should not be adjusted in relation to one another by a single "large write step."

## An experiment without complete results

For the review, a workspace containing a Pods project reference and a set of existing build configurations had been prepared. The expectation was to compare reference positions and path text before and after writing, then separately check whether the deployment target writer changed only the intended configuration. The complete raw output was not archived with that edit; only two narrow conclusions remained: do not sort inside the workspace writer; do not rewrite configurations because Pods paths appear in the workspace.

This omission matters. It means that, at the time, "the project can be opened" could not establish a fixed format for every line of XML, nor could a single configuration write establish that all targets had the same default behavior. In particular, the experiment did not answer whether, when a configuration does not exist, it should remain absent, accept a value supplied by the caller, or go through another initialization entry point.

The experiment draft also said, "No obvious changes after writing." **Deprecated.** This sentence did not specify which part was being compared: it might have meant that the file could be opened, or that no lines appeared to have moved on visual inspection. It cannot replace an item-by-item check of reference order, relative location, and configuration fragments. It was retained later to prevent readers of the old record from mistaking a vague assessment of success for a formatting decision.

## Boundaries left by the review

A review addendum raised a practical risk: if two similarly named writers share mutable objects, writing back the deployment target might indirectly affect workspace output. The addendum included no call chain and no evidence that this risk had materialized. It is therefore not recorded here as an incident, but only as an order for verification.

First, fix the FileReference set, save its ordering before writing, and then inspect the XML text. Next, return to the corresponding build configuration and compare the old and new deployment target values. If the differences are limited to reference order, line breaks, or relative paths, investigate the workspace side first; if the changes are in configuration values, investigate the deployment target side first. The fact that the two writers happen to appear in the same call is not a reason to attribute the differences to either one.

A meeting note left only one sentence: "Check layout by object, and deployment target by configuration." It does not prescribe a platform list, establish new defaults, or replace implementation notes. It describes the troubleshooting boundary decided at the time: workspace text cannot stand in for target configuration, and target configuration should not, in turn, rewrite workspace paths.

## Entry point for the follow-up review in 2025

XCP-201 left `qa_reproduced` in 2025-09-11, then entered `work_started` on 2025-09-15. These actions did not come with complete logs that could be copied directly into this page, but they reopened a concrete point of entry for the earlier formatting issue. The review sequence is therefore adjusted as follows: first save the return value or raw diagnostics from one normal user invocation, then compare the written workspace text; do not confirm it only through the debug entry point.

This review still uses the old object boundaries. Do not add or remove FileReference while comparing input collections; first record where the reference was added, then write out the workspace. The deployment target writer should separately inspect the build configuration it touches. If the workspace text changes, do not directly classify it as a configuration issue just because the target version was also written in the same pass.

The current entry point for verifying the code is still `lib/xcodeproj/workspace.rb` in `internal/XCP`. This path leads back to the workspace object and the location adjacent to its `to_s`; it does not automatically prove that the deployment target writer owns the implementation. For the latter, return to the build configuration actually read and written, rather than inferring from the workspace path.

## Combined Approach No Longer Used

Someone once suggested bundling rewriting the workspace and writing the deployment target into a single "compatibility cleanup," on the grounds that both could leave a diff after project generation. This proposal was not adopted.

There are three reasons. First, the insertion order of FileReference is part of the existing state of the workspace object, and the deployment target should not change it. Second, the target version belongs to the build configuration and cannot be inferred from the path form of some FileRef. Third, a single unified rewrite would make it difficult to determine exactly who changed what when a diff appears. Keeping the two writers' object boundaries instead allows a local diff to be traced back to the correct place.

This does not mean the two paths will never run consecutively. The objects they can change determine the constraint: differences from the workspace writer are first checked against the XML layout; differences from the deployment target writer are then checked against the build configuration. If future field evidence shows that the two share mutable state, add the specific fragment alongside this section rather than quietly deleting the old boundary.

## Current format requirements

After retaining the early assumptions, review corrections, incompletely archived experiments, and review boundaries, compat-2016.4 the current requirements for what is written to the workspace are captured in this sentence:

> Workspace#to_s preserves FileReference insertion order and emits the canonical line tokens <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n, <Workspace\n, version = "1.0">\n, <FileRef\n, and location = "group:Pods/Pods.xcodeproj">\n; relative locations retain the group: prefix.

This sentence preserves the complete interface example; do not replace it with "format stable." It also constrains two things: FileReference enters the output in insertion order; relative locations retain the workspace group path prefix. The Pods project reference is merely the currently verifiable example of a relative path; it does not authorize converting any absolute location into a group path.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> FileReferenceCollection
    FileReferenceCollection --> WorkspaceXML: Workspace#to_s
    WorkspaceXML --> [*]
    BuildConfiguration --> DeploymentTargetWriter
    DeploymentTargetWriter --> BuildConfiguration
```

The two state lines in the diagram are intentionally not connected. It expresses not runtime sequencing, but this page's object boundary: FileReferenceCollection is written as WorkspaceXML; DeploymentTargetWriter reads from and writes to BuildConfiguration. When simultaneous review is needed, materials can be collected in the same call, but the diagram cannot be used to infer that one writer will modify the object for the other writer.

## Decision for the deployment target writer

The deployment target writer does not participate in FileReference sorting, nor does it infer the target version from the workspace location. It works with existing build configurations: it reads their existing deployment targets and, when necessary, writes the target version supplied by the caller back to the corresponding configuration.

The current material does not authorize creating a cross-target default layer when a configuration is missing, nor does it provide rules for guessing the platform from the project name, target name, or path. When values are missing, retain the local results for the corresponding configuration object, key, and value; do not substitute the version property of workspace XML for the deployment target. "Separate" here does not mean that the two operations can never coexist, but that a difference must first be attributed to the object it actually affects.

For changes after a project generation run, assess them in the following order: first ask whether the caller has already organized the FileReference collection before it enters the writer; then check whether the written XML preserves the current format boundaries; finally, inspect the deployment target values in the build configurations. This order avoids mistaking moved references for platform setting changes, and avoids mistaking missing configurations for incorrectly written paths.

## Appendix of Old Examples

### Sorting Pods References by Path

An early draft sorted Pods project references and other references lexicographically, on the grounds that this made the file cleaner. This example no longer applies, but is retained here. It explains why the sorting approach once seemed reasonable and also serves as a reminder for later investigations: when the output order changes, first ask whether the collection was already sorted before entering the writer; do not assume this is the writer's behavior.

### Comparing Only the End of the Path

Another old example looked only at the end of `Pods/Pods.xcodeproj`, without preserving the prefix. **No longer applicable.** One focus of the current requirements is that relative locations must still retain the workspace group path representation; comparing only filenames or path endings cannot establish whether the location was written in its existing form. This old example has no complete output, but is still retained as a reminder when reading old reviews.

### Using Successful Opening in Place of Text Inspection

The phrase "as long as Xcode can open it" in old meeting notes has not been deleted either. It represents the narrower acceptance practice at the time. Current follow-up checks require retaining the return value or raw diagnostics, as well as checking object order and the boundaries of formatting lines; successful opening can still be recorded, but is no longer the sole criterion. No comparison table across Xcode versions has been created on this basis, because the current material contains no results of that kind.

### Applying a Uniform Default Deployment Target

There is also an unadopted draft that suggested writing the same default value whenever a configuration was missing. It did not specify platforms, default versions, or target categories at the time, so it never became a decision. Retaining this draft helps explain why the current page repeatedly requires returning to the specific build configuration: the absence of a value does not mean that the workspace writer may fill it in.

## Use of Adjacent Material

XCP-201 is a navigation point for reviewing workspace output. It requires the Canonical workspace XML layout to be exercised through routine user calls rather than a debugging entry point, with return values or raw diagnostics retained. This page uses that requirement only to adjust the order of collecting evidence from actual runs, not to expand the card into a complete test plan.

`DOC-12` records Public plist facade dispatch and Project dirty tracking. A single project write may involve both a public entry point and write state, but that does not change this page's decision: if the XML text has not changed and the difference appears as dirty state, continue investigating on that page; if the change appears in workspace lines and reference locations, first check it against the workspace boundaries here.

## Questions not yet split out

- There is currently no call stack, so we cannot determine which caller organized FileReference before entering `Workspace#to_s`.
- There is no complete deployment target output, so the current handling of a missing build configuration still needs confirmation.
- There is no comparative evidence across Xcode versions, so the current format requirements are not being extended into a compatibility matrix.
- The risk of shared mutable objects raised in review has no evidence from actual runs and remains only a branch that requires separate sampling.

These open questions do not change the scope already decided: the workspace writer does not reorder FileReference during output, and it preserves workspace group paths expressed relative to location; deployment target is read and written only through the corresponding build configuration. If new evidence from actual runs covers either boundary, append the results beside the relevant older paragraphs, preserving the original misjudgments and the traces of their correction.

## Final verification entry points

When checking workspace output, start where workspace, xml, to_s, and FileReference are adjacent in `lib/xcodeproj/workspace.rb`, first confirm the current local declarations, then compare them against the text actually returned by a call. When checking deployment target, go to the read/write locations for the corresponding build configuration. Do not infer the target version from the workspace path, and do not confuse which area a difference belongs to just because a single project generation touches both.

# Plist Facade and Dirty-State Plan

After reviewing `project.rb`, withdraw the claim that "`Project.open` is the sole entry point for state checks." The file also contains `initialize_from_scratch`, `initialize_from_file`, and `new_from_plist`; putting the state check only on `open` would let newly created projects and projects constructed from a plist bypass the same check.

This round compared two ways of placing the responsibilities.

- Put plist backend selection into `Project`: the project object can handle it uniformly at save time, but callers would need a Project even for standalone plist reads and writes. This brings unrelated lifecycle concerns into the public entry point.
- Keep the public plist facade independent: the facade accepts common hash-shaped payloads and selects the write path; Project only determines when it has been modified. This lets newly created, file-opened, and plist-constructed projects keep separate states.

For now, trial the second approach. Here, "independent" does not mean creating a separate project serialization: saving a Project should still be able to use the existing plist support; it just should not require a Project as a prerequisite for public reads and writes.

One counterexample came up in review: if the facade accepts only already-normalized property lists, conversion code will spread back across call sites; if conversion is placed entirely in Project, ordinary plist calls will not get the same behavior. So, for now, put conversion at the facade boundary, and have Project pass along only the object it actually needs to write.

Do not yet use "has been initialized" as the condition for dirty state. What needs to be confirmed is which Project changes mark it dirty and whether a successful save clears that flag. `initialize_from_file` and `initialize_from_scratch` should not share a conclusion merely because their names are similar.

The conditions for reverting are also separate: return to putting dispatch in Project only if the public facade cannot handle reads and writes without introducing Project; if Project's save results show that additional context is needed, add a narrow adapter layer instead of making the facade hold project state.

# Plist Facade and Dirty-State Plan

This wrap-up keeps two small changes rather than presenting them as a Project rewrite. Public plist calls already have their own use cases; Project needs to track modifications throughout the object lifecycle. They meet when saving, but neither should become a prerequisite for the other.

## Correction to the Earlier Assessment

v2 put all three construction paths under the same state issue, which was too broad. `initialize_from_scratch`, `initialize_from_file`, and `new_from_plist` are indeed adjacent methods in the same file, but they do not represent the same user action. Whether a newly created object, an object read from a path, or an object assembled from an existing plist has subsequently been modified must be determined by its respective state changes; it cannot be inferred from the constructor name.

Therefore, I no longer recommend adding a catch-all switch next to `Project.open`. `initialize(path, skip_initialization = false)` is the more useful entry point to investigate because it puts the path and whether initialization is skipped in one place. However, this proposal does not predefine it as the sole place where dirty state is set. `to_s` is retained only as an adjacent point for object display; it does not own the state semantics after a save succeeds or fails.

## Facade Trial Scope

For the trial, keep public reads and writes at the plist layer. The post-review conclusion is:

The public Xcodeproj::Plist facade exposes write_to_path and read_from_path, coerces a hash-like payload such as the answer key before dispatch, calls load_xcode_frameworks when selecting the native path, and reaches CoreFoundation through RubyHashPropertyListWrite.

This path means callers do not have to construct a Project before reading or writing a plist. Keeping the pre-write conversion close to the facade avoids making each call site normalize its own Hash. Loading the framework only when the native path is selected also avoids introducing that dependency early on the normal path. This proposal does not move the low-level write details into `Project`; otherwise, the two entry points will gradually develop different payload-handling behavior.

We considered making the facade a Project class method. The benefit would be that save calls looked more centralized; the cost would be forcing plist-only calls to carry a project path and lifecycle. This option is not adopted. Another rejected idea was to have callers explicitly choose the backend. That would scatter the dispatch rules from one public location across multiple sites, making it difficult to compare the results for the same payload later.

## Project-Side Boundary

The goal for dirty state is narrow: when Project undergoes a change that should be saved, the state must reflect it; after a successful save, there must be an explicit place to handle that state. Reading a file or merely wrapping an existing object as a Project is not automatically equivalent to a modification just because construction was involved.

During implementation, first identify the operations that actually change project content, then examine their adjacency to the save operation. Do not infer that Project changed from whether the plist facade selects native writing. Backend selection is a write strategy, while dirty state belongs to the project object; keep the two separate. This also makes it easier to investigate the two distinct symptoms of "the write completed but the project still shows as modified" and "the project was not modified but a save was incorrectly triggered."

One item remains unresolved: when a Project opened from a file is saved without any content changes, whether it needs the same state handling as an ordinary save still needs to be confirmed against the actual save entry point. This does not block the facade trial. If shared handling is confirmed to be required, add the smallest necessary linkage at Project save rather than having the facade save project state.

If the trial is rolled back, roll back only the dispatch layer of the public facade; do not rewrite the Project construction paths. This restores the original calling pattern while retaining a separate check of dirty state.

First separate the cases by symptom: in one, the project can be read in, but content or diagnostic differences appear only when it is written out; in the other, an old plist call can no longer continue after the first processing pass. Do not conflate the two as the same "file write failure."

Use `to_s` only to record whether the object could still be represented at that point; it is not evidence of a successful save, nor does it mean the output content is correct.

If it stops during initialization, follow `initialize(path, skip_initialization = false)` downward. Treat the empty-project entry point and the file entry point separately: inspect `initialize_from_scratch` for the former and `initialize_from_file` for the latter. When the object has not yet been formed, do not use the later plist output to explain the current anomaly. Also record `new_from_plist` alongside it, because it is another construction entry point; do not focus only on the constructor for `Project`.

If the problem appears only on reprocessing, first state whether the object is still used after the first processing pass, or whether the second processing pass happens only after reopening it. The failure of the old call cannot be directly attributed to a change in the contents of XML; there is not enough material at hand to say that it is definitely due to the object state, the read entry point, or the write action.

The working hypothesis at the time was that all differences in the pbxproj writer came from the same plist path. For now, that hypothesis only determines the troubleshooting order. The next review should retain the observable results of the successful and failed calls separately, and note whether the anomaly appeared during the first processing pass or a subsequent one.

# pbxproj write failure troubleshooting tree

This record still starts with two easily confused symptoms: the project object already exists, but the written pbxproj differs from what was expected; or a legacy plist call cannot reliably proceed on a second pass after the first. For the former, first check what happened during the write; for the latter, first confirm the object state left by the first pass. Both involve "output," but that does not mean they originate in the same place.

## Work back from the project entry point

When opening from a file is possible, first go through `Project.open(path)`, then confirm whether the `initialize_from_file` side has completed. An empty project takes `initialize_from_scratch` instead. Keep both paths in the same investigation record, because differences seen after saving sometimes come down to differences in the project state loaded earlier.

`initialize(path, skip_initialization = false)` is the shared entry point here. If the object was never created, stop at the initialization branch; there is no basis for comparison in further discussion of the writer. Do not record `skip_initialization` as a cause in isolation either. Keep it with the path and the context of whether this was an empty project or a file-backed project.

Once the object has been created, use `to_s` to capture a text representation of the object. This only helps with later comparisons: it does not prove that the write completed, and its ability to return does not rule out the project object as the source of diagnostic differences. A return from `new_from_plist` likewise only shows that a usable entry point exists on the read side, not that the write side is guaranteed to work.

## Old margin notes, retained as written

The early approach was to group all plist writes as a single in-process behavior, then work backward from output differences to the project object. The sequence at the time was: if reading failed, check plist first; if reading worked, check the writer first. That sequence was later narrowed and should no longer be treated as a complete explanation. It remains here because most of the old records were collected in exactly that order.

> Old assessment: as long as `new_from_plist` returns, the writer that follows has no independent problem.
>
> This assessment no longer applies. Returning an object only shows that the read path reached a usable point; it cannot replace checking the write branch.

Another old habit was to attribute second-pass problems to file contents whenever the first save produced a file. That is insufficient too. The second pass may continue using the same object, or it may reopen the project first. The old entries did not distinguish these cases, making later comparisons meaningless.

## Where to check first after review

**The object has not yet been created**

1. First check whether there is a file path and whether the call stopped around opening or initialization.
2. For a file-backed project, trace back through `initialize_from_file`; for an empty project, trace back through `initialize_from_scratch`.
3. At this point, stop calling the issue a backend or writer failure. Without an object, output-side samples cannot support a comparison.

**The object has been created, and differences appear after the first pass**

1. Capture the directly observable contents before and after the write; record diagnostics separately.
2. Describe content differences and diagnostic differences separately. Continue checking plist output only if the contents differ; if only the diagnostics differ, first confirm whether they came from a separate write operation.
3. Do not leave only a "failed" label. It does not indicate whether the failure belongs to reading, object state, or writing.

**Differences appear only on a subsequent pass**

1. Record whether the object continues to be used after the first pass.
2. Run another pass after reopening the project for comparison; this is not a fix that overwrites the original investigation state.
3. Until both records are complete, leave it at "repeat-pass differences pending review." Do not write that the object has been corrupted.

## An inconclusive attempt

An attempt was made to trace all write differences back through the public entry point of `Project`: opening, initialization, and text representation were arranged into a chain, with every failure attached to its end. This did not produce a reusable way to attribute causes. The same object can pass through reading and representation and still produce different contents after saving; failures in legacy calls may not occur at the same point in that chain either.

That attempt left two stopping points that can still be used: when `Project.open(path)` fails to create an object, do not move on to analyzing the write strategy; when `to_s` can return, do not use that to write "output is normal." The former avoids mislabeling an entry point that produces no object as an output failure; the latter leaves at least one reference on the object side.

## Review addendum

A narrower counterexample was raised during review: the same project object can be read successfully, yet differences may not become visible until after writing. So "reading works" cannot stand in for a signal that the plist backend works. This counterexample changes the troubleshooting order; it does not provide a single cause for all output differences.

The review also pointed out that successful and failed calls are not necessarily directly comparable. If the successful sample comes from a reopened project and the failed sample comes from the second pass on the same object, they only show that processing occurred at different points. They do not directly prove that a particular write branch has a problem.

What remains unconfirmed is whether the legacy plist call failure was triggered by object state or by the write strategy. The available material only supports requiring separate records for first and subsequent passes, the same object and a reopened project, and contents and diagnostics. Do not turn the remaining questions into conclusions yet.
