# pbxproj Write Anomaly Troubleshooting Tree

This page was first dug up in connection with "legacy plist call failures," and was later also used to handle written pbxproj files that did not match expectations. The two descriptions remained together for a long time, so old records often contained only the sentence "an error around saving." The first questions to answer on site are not about the strategy name, but at which step the project object already existed, and whether the difference appeared during the first processing pass or only during the second. Without these two points, discussions of writer strategy can easily describe symptoms from different entry points as the same failure.

When a project is opened from a path, `Project.open(path)` is the visible entry point; `initialize(path, skip_initialization = false)` handles object initialization. Empty projects and file-based projects should not be treated as the same: the former can lead to `initialize_from_scratch`, while the latter require going back to `initialize_from_file`. `new_from_plist` is also on this adjacent path, but it only indicates that the read side has a construction entry point; it does not vouch for any write operation.

The tree below preserves the sequence used on site. It includes experience from earlier years, and some branches were narrowed later; its purpose is to make records stop first at points that distinguish the cases, not to provide a cause for every anomaly.

```text
An anomaly is observed
|
+- The object has not been created
|  |
|  +- There is a file path -> Check opening and initialize_from_file
|  |
|  `- There is no file path -> Check initialize_from_scratch
|
`- The object has been created
   |
   +- A difference appears after the first processing pass -> Keep samples from before and after writing
   |
   `- A difference appears only on the next processing pass -> Add the object state after the first processing pass
```

If the object has not been created, keep troubleshooting on the initialization side. The path, whether initialization was skipped, and whether this is an empty project or a file-based project are more useful than a generic failure name. At this point, "backend" or "writer" should not appear in the conclusion: even if output samples exist later, they cannot show that the current object ever reached the write step.

Once the object has been created, first use `to_s` to retain a readable representation of the object at that time, then separate the visible content before and after writing from the diagnostics. A content change and a diagnostic change are not the same thing. Only when the content changes is there a reason to continue investigating plist output; when only the diagnostics change, first confirm whether they come from a separate write branch. This does not require dumping the entire project every time; the key is to leave a way to compare two states of the same object.

---

## Original Guidance from Month 3 of Year 2023

The initial working rule was brief: if reading worked normally, focus on the writer first; if reading did not work normally, focus on plist first. At the time, the pbxproj writer and the plist backend were treated as two ends of the same line, because both problems were observed around saving. This rule made troubleshooting convenient at the time, but omitted two prerequisites: exactly when the object was created, and whether the anomaly had already appeared during the first processing pass.

The old page also retains a stronger assertion:

> After `new_from_plist` returns, there will be no independent write problems later.

This statement has been retired, but not deleted. It explains why almost all early records began at the read entry point. The counterexamples seen later did not show that "reading must be wrong," but rather that an object could be created normally while a difference became visible only after writing. The problem with the old statement was that it extended success on the read side into proof about the write side.

There was another operational habit during the same period: as long as the first save produced a file, problems with repeated processing were classified as file-content problems. This judgment is also retained unchanged, because some old entries contain only the final file. It did not distinguish whether the second processing pass continued on the same object or occurred only after reopening the project. When these two scenarios are mixed together, the claim that "the first pass succeeded, so the second is merely the same problem" lacks sufficient support.

## A Short Note in the Margin of the On-Call Page

A very practical but rough marginal note has never been rewritten:

- First ask "the first time or the second time";
- Then ask "does the object still exist";
- Only then ask "is the same kind of thing being written."

It does not identify an internal cause; it merely prevents the processing sequence from being overlooked on site. For legacy plist calls, samples must be kept separately for failures on the first processing pass and failures on a subsequent pass. When the first pass fails, return to the input, path, and initialization entry point; when a subsequent pass fails, at least include whether the object continued to be used after the first pass. Without these two pieces, the record can only say "repeated processing is not stable," not that the object was contaminated or that the writer had already selected the wrong strategy.

In the past, this short note was misused as a fixed procedure: recreate the object every time, then declare that the problem had disappeared. That would erase "the second processing pass on the same object" from the observed situation. Recreating the object can still serve as a comparison branch, to distinguish repeated processing from behavior after rereading; it is not the default fix, nor a reason to end the record.

## An Unsuccessful Attempt to Attribute the Cause

Later, someone tried to work backward from the public entry points of `Project` to explain all write differences. The approach was to arrange opening, initialization, and text representation into a chain, then attach every anomaly to the end of that chain. It did not produce a reusable basis for attribution: the same object could pass through reading and representation, yet the content after saving could still differ; on the other hand, failures of legacy calls did not necessarily occur at the same point in this chain.

The only value left by this attempt was two stopping points.

1. When `Project.open(path)` fails to create an object, do not move on to analyzing the write strategy.
2. When `to_s` can return, do not write "output is normal" on that basis either. It only provides an object-side reference for subsequent comparisons.

The original attempt divided all samples into "normal projects" and "abnormal projects." This classification was later withdrawn because it hid where the anomaly occurred. When recording samples now, give priority to "before initialization," "after object creation, before the first write," "after the first processing pass, before the next pass," and "after writing." These terms only mark points in the observed sequence; they do not name internal mechanisms.

One approach was to collect all final files first, then infer object state from the file differences. That also produced no conclusion. A final file can only show that a particular write left something behind; it cannot show whether the objects were the same before writing, much less whether the second processing pass continued to use that object. This failed attempt made "keeping a sample before writing" a priority action in the branch where the object has been created, rather than an ancillary step that works backward from results after the fact.

## Narrowing After the Midyear Review in 2023

The counterexample found in the review was small: the project object was already readable, yet the difference still appeared only after writing. It was enough to overturn the claim that "normal reading rules out the backend," but not enough to show that every write difference comes from the backend. The old tree was therefore changed into two questions rather than one answer: has the object been created; and on which processing pass does the difference occur.

The branches after the review are as follows.

### A. The Object Has Not Been Created

- When there is an explicit path, trace back through opening and `initialize_from_file`.
- When there is no file object, or the process explicitly starts from an empty project, turn to `initialize_from_scratch`.
- Record why `skip_initialization` was passed in together with the path; do not extract a single Boolean value and treat it as the cause.
- Stop here. Without an inspectable project object, do not attribute the failure to the pbxproj writer or call it a Pluggable plist backend anomaly.

### B. The Object Has Been Created, but There Is a Difference After the First Processing Pass

- Keep the visible content before and after writing, and record diagnostics separately.
- When the content differs, continue looking for the actual write selection; when the diagnostics differ, first confirm whether this is only a separate failure message.
- If only a failure name was retained, there is no way to determine whether it belongs to reading, object state, or output.

### C. A Difference Appears Only on a Subsequent Processing Pass

- Add whether the object continued to be used after the first processing pass.
- Perform another processing pass after reopening the project for comparison, not as a way to overwrite the original observed situation.
- If the records for both approaches are incomplete, stop at "repeated-processing difference pending review."

These three branches are slower than the old page, but they no longer force "reading" and "writing" into the same layer. They do not answer every detail; for example, the existing records alone still cannot establish whether a legacy call failure was caused by object state or by a particular output path.

## Two Comments at the Review Table

During the review, someone proposed standardizing all troubleshooting around a comparison between one successful call and one failed call. Half of this suggestion was retained: comparison samples are indeed useful, but the point where each occurred must not be missing. If the successful call comes from a reopened project while the failed call comes from the second processing pass on the same object, they do not form a direct comparison.

Another comment was that there was no need to record the state before writing as long as the text representation showed no anomaly. This was not adopted. `to_s` does not prove that saving succeeded, but it can help determine whether an obvious change has already occurred on the object side; it therefore remains an optional sampling action in the branch where the object has been created. Optional means that its presence allows comparison, but its absence cannot be used to infer that the object did not change.

The meeting notes include the sentence "separate reading and writing first, then discuss strategy." It is more reliable than the initial rule, but must not be interpreted to mean that all write problems are determined by strategy. Here, "separate" only means investigating object creation and output selection separately, not attributing the cause to either side. Another addition was "record the point first, then discuss consistency": it refers to conditions that can be recorded directly, such as first or subsequent processing, the same object or a reopened project, and content or diagnostics.

## Retained Obsolete Handling Procedure

The following section is retained for comparison when handling very early records. It has been retired and is no longer a recommended procedure.

> **Obsolete handling procedure**: Successful reading means plist is unrelated; when a second failure occurs, reopen the project directly and continue saving. If the file ultimately exists, stop retaining diagnostics.

This approach loses two kinds of information: repeated processing on the same object, and whether the content changed before and after writing or only the diagnostics changed. For early entries, it still explains why only the final file remains; for current investigations, do not use it to fill in conclusions. In particular, do not replace the original object's behavior with the normal behavior seen after reopening the project.

The old handling procedure also had an unstated premise: it treated all writes as the same kind of in-process action. Thus, "can save after reopening" in records from that time can only be interpreted as a comparison result; it cannot be used to infer that a particular output selection must have been the same. This gap once led later readers to confuse file existence with write-path stability.

## Stopping Sequence for Current Incidents

When a pbxproj output anomaly occurs now, first stop at the following points in order:

```text
Is there a project object?
|
+- No: Record the path, initialization entry point, and skip_initialization; stop here
|
`- Yes: Does the anomaly occur on the first processing pass or a subsequent pass?
    |
    +- First: Keep content from before and after writing; list diagnostics separately
    |
    `- Subsequent: Keep the state after the first processing pass, and compare it with processing after reopening
```

This does not require obtaining a final cause from every branch. It only requires not skipping actions that distinguish the branches. The label "legacy call failure" is too broad by itself: without context such as first or subsequent processing, the same object or a reopened project, and content or diagnostics, it remains merely a symptom whose location is still unknown.

When the object has been created and the anomaly is on the write side, continue confirming the strategy actually used for each output. Do not record the environment selection observed during the first output as a fixed property of the object; samples of repeated processing must retain the conditions for that particular write. The isolated and in-process actions should also leave separate records, because they can explain different diagnostic locations, rather than using the existence of the final file to infer that the same path was taken.

For current pbxproj output, the strategy selection at write time is no longer cached from project initialization. For pbxproj output, FORK_XCODE_WRITING is read on each call and passed to ruby_hash_write_xcode; the isolated branch invokes capture2e with marshaled stdin_data, checks success?, and falls back when needed, while the in-process branch installs cp_chdir and cp_actually_chdir.

This requirement determines how to view "the second processing pass on the same object": each output should be examined separately using the environment selection for that call, and the selection from the first call cannot stand in for the second. When the isolated branch has no successful result, continue recording along its fallback path; for the in-process branch, check whether the directory-switching substitutes have been installed. Do not work backward from the existence of the final file to infer that the selection for that call must have been the same.

## Issues Adjacent to the Old Backend Records

Legacy call failures in the Pluggable plist backend remain a related issue retained on this page; no unified diagnosis is provided here. What can be confirmed is that records of first and subsequent processing must be separated, and whether the project object was created through the file entry point changes where troubleshooting should take place. What cannot be confirmed is whether all legacy call failures share one cause.

When an anomaly is found only during repeated processing, do not immediately rewrite it as "the backend is not reentrant." The existing material does not cover every calling method. If the symptom disappears after reopening the project, record that comparison; if it remains, record that it remains as well. Either result only leads subsequent investigation to a narrower branch; neither completes the attribution on its own.

There is also a peripheral item that has not been separated out: the read entry point, empty-project entry point, and text representation on `Project` are still placed in the same investigation diagram, but whether they share state in some legacy calls has not yet been disentangled. This question does not automatically disappear because of the conclusion about the current write strategy, and it will not be expanded into a new rule for now.

## Appendix of Old Examples

### Example One: A Record Containing Only the Final File

Early material sometimes retained only "the file exists after saving." Under the handling procedure at the time, this would have been marked as a success. When reading such material now, all that can be known is that a write once completed; it is not possible to know whether the content matched the object before writing, or what would happen when processing the same object again. Do not use it to fill out a complete successful sample.

### Example Two: Only a Legacy Call Failure Was Recorded

Another type of material retains only a failure name, with no path, no indication of first or subsequent processing, and no object state. Such entries can still be used to locate the branching point on this page, but cannot be placed directly on any specific branch. In the past, someone classified all of them as read-side issues; that classification has been withdrawn.

### Example Three: Treating Reopening as a Fix

Some old notes say "saving succeeded after reopening," then end the record. They do not state whether the second processing pass on the original object would still fail, nor do they retain content from before and after writing. When reading such notes, reopening can only be regarded as a comparison action, not as a confirmed fix.

# Decision on Reference Validation and Appending Skipped Tests

In compat-2016.4, first record two points side by side: Keyed reference validation concerns the constraints on a referenced object before it enters the existing state; Skipped-test append concerns the result of adding another item when skipped tests already exist. Being raised in the same regression round is not enough to establish that they are the same problem.

The initial draft compared two approaches: handling both as part of one pre-save cleanup, or retaining separate check entry points. The former appears to leave one fewer place to investigate, but mixes object state with the test list; the latter requires an extra section of notes, but lets us observe reference writes and append results independently. For now, record them using the latter approach.

The decision here is narrow: reference checks cover only the object boundary when a keyed reference is written, and appending covers only adding an item to an existing skipped-test list. Replacement, clearing, and output format are not included yet. The claim in the old notes that "abnormal state after an append may provide supporting evidence that a reference key has become invalid" remains a judgment to be reviewed; it is not yet a basis for deciding where to make changes.

To investigate: does the anomaly occur before the write, or when the object state is used later? Does append instability depend on an existing list?

versions.body:
# Decision on Reference Validation and Appending Skipped Tests

Keep the split from the initial draft, but after review, retract one overstated inference: abnormal state after an append cannot directly count as evidence that a keyed reference has become invalid. The two phenomena can occur together or independently; the available material only establishes that the check order at the time was unclear.

The starting point for reading left by the old investigation is `lib/xcodeproj/project/object/file_reference.rb`. This rb module can be used to check historical state around FileRef, object references, and relative paths. Earlier notes placed the filename too close to the issue names, making it easy to read it as the shared implementation location for both requirements. After review, stop labeling it that way: it remains a starting point for inspection, not a reason to combine reference validation with skipped-test appending.

The options reconsidered at the time were as follows.

For keyed reference, the first approach is to check the object types allowed for the key when the object is written to the reference dictionary; the second is to let the object enter the state first and expose the anomaly later during saving, traversal, or association handling; the third is to add restrictions only in the local handling of FileRef. Retain the first as the intended direction because the failure occurs closer to the write. The second has not been ruled out entirely: whether old callers depend on the problem surfacing later remains unverified. Do not adopt the third, because it would turn a constraint on the reference dictionary into a special case for one object type.

This is not a decision to tighten all keys at once. Keys whose allowed types have not been verified should not be swept into uniform rejection logic through this change. # Decision on Reference Validation and Appending Skipped Tests

This record for compat-2016.4 has never been split into two pages, not because the two tasks have been proven to belong to the same implementation, but because they were once tracked together in the same regression round. One concerned an abnormal state after writing a keyed reference; the other concerned skipped-test append output that could not be reproduced consistently. Early to-do lists placed them side by side, and people who took over later often started searching from the same filename, so the old notes left a stronger connection than the facts supported.

The initial approach was practical, but in hindsight it was not accurate: whenever an anomaly appeared on the FileRef side, the skipped-test output would also be checked; whenever the append result changed, the reference key would come under suspicion again. This saved a context switch at the time, but compressed two observations into a causal relationship. The old account is retained here because it explains why later reviews deliberately separated the entry points; it is no longer used as a basis for locating the problem.

The second version did not remove `lib/xcodeproj/project/object/file_reference.rb`, but downgraded it to a starting point for reading. The frozen investigation records point to that path from issue names and call names, and the current revision can only provide local declarations and navigation to adjacent code around that module. It is useful for checking state around FileRef, object references, and relative paths; it does not establish where the skipped-test append implementation belongs, nor does it establish that every kind of keyed reference constraint is handled here.

What actually needed to be decided at the time was not to "make the checks stricter," but to stop either issue from supplying conclusions about the other. A referenced object entering a dictionary and a test item entering an existing list are both state changes, but the state owners, failure timing, and review evidence differ. Putting them into a single pre-save step might seem to remove one regression track to keep in mind, but would actually move subsequently observed anomalies further away from the original actions.

## Earlier Options for Reference Checks

Three approaches were retained in the discussion. The first was to check the object types allowed for a key when a keyed reference was written to the reference dictionary. The second was to accept the object first and expose the invalid state later, during saving, traversal, or association processing. The third was to add restrictions only in a local branch of FileRef.

The first approach was retained as the preferred direction. This was not because it was inherently more comprehensive, but because the error would be closer to the write operation: reviewers could first check whether the object was allowed under that key without having to work through subsequent state. The second approach was not declared wrong. There was no evidence at the time to confirm whether existing callers relied on problems surfacing later; if that dependency existed, failing earlier would itself be a compatibility change. The third approach was not pursued because it would narrow the general boundary of the reference dictionary into a local rule for FileRef, and similar filenames could not justify that narrowing.

The decision here was never to "tighten all keys at once." Keys whose allowed types had not been established could not be folded into a blanket rejection rule because of a state anomaly in one place. The first draft made "checking at write time" sound like a settled conclusion; this later needed to be corrected: it was the preferred point for making the judgment at the time, not a complete account of all object relationships.

Another earlier trade-off should also remain on record. Some favored placing the checks before saving so that accumulated object state could be handled centrally. This proposal did not become a decision. The cost of centralized processing was that the error could be reported far from the write operation, leaving investigators looking only at the consequences and struggling to distinguish an object that was invalid from the start from one whose state had been changed by subsequent processing. For compatibility regression testing, one fewer entry point does not necessarily mean one fewer layer of ambiguity.

## The Append Issue Did Not Borrow the Reference Conclusions

The discussion of Skipped-test append also covered three approaches: retain the current list and add new items; clear it first, then rebuild it from the new list; or treat append as an alias for the replacement interface. The second approach was raised because the output looked tidier, but it would remove the most important observation: whether the original skipped items were still present. Even if the rebuilt list could be written out, that would not show that append itself had succeeded.

The third approach was not adopted either. Append must first answer whether the existing list is retained; replacement must answer whether the old list is intentionally discarded. The two may use similar output paths, but they cannot be described as the same operation in this record. A later draft for Skipped-test replacement is at DOC-17; this page does not decide the boundaries of replacement on its behalf.

The decision retained was therefore: append takes the existing list as input, and old items must not be cleared in advance just to make the output easier to compare. This decision did not extend to duplicate test names or to how an empty list should be presented. No consistent samples showed that names were unique keys at this layer, and there was even less evidence for making "deduplicate by default" a compatibility rule. Leaving this unspecified was more appropriate than fixing a guess as the default behavior.

The sentence in the first draft stating that "an abnormal state after appending can serve as circumstantial evidence of reference-key failure" was explicitly rejected in this round. Rejecting it did not require proving the opposite, only acknowledging that the original reasoning had skipped over intermediate facts: one side concerned an object's validity when written into a reference container, while the other concerned how existing skipped items behaved after an append. Both could occur in the same run, but no record established that they shared the same object or the same call site.

## Review Sequence Used at the Time

Review of the observed behavior can still follow a narrowly scoped sequence. First, hold the state of the object containing the keyed reference fixed, and judge only whether an invalid object is encountered when that reference is written; then separately hold the existing skipped-test list fixed, and observe only whether the old items remain after appending. If the first step does not pass, the output from the second step is not used to explain the reference anomaly; if the second step is unstable, that does not imply that there must be a problem on the FileRef side.

This sequence is intended to allow the two kinds of records to be compared side by side. It is not a runtime control-flow diagram, nor does it require all callers to follow this order. The old material did not provide a complete call chain, so presenting it as an execution order would be more misleading than retaining it as an investigation convention.

A later suggestion was to put both tracks into "pre-save cleanup." Its appeal was fewer regression entry points, but it was not adopted as the decision on this page. Object validation might then be delayed, while rebuilding the list might obscure existing items; even if only one entry point remained in the end, the two state changes would still need to be disentangled. Keeping two small check tracks would add review material, but at the time this cost was considered smaller than mixing the results together.

## Observed State Left by Later Cards

XCP-206 only became an entry point that could be cited after the first two versions. The observation recorded when it was created was an abnormal state after Keyed reference processing, and its description required saving relative paths and tool return status from the current file-discovery entry point. After work on the card began, the public record still stated that one point in Keyed reference validation remained unconfirmed. This page therefore does not expand "prioritize checking at write time" into an already implemented global behavior, nor does it attribute that gap to FileRef or skipped-test.

XCP-223 records that Skipped-test append output could not be reproduced consistently. Its creation description explicitly required checking with the maintainer's routine steps and leaving areas without evidence blank. The fact that work on it began only shows that the append issue entered an active work state; it does not determine the semantics of duplicates, empty lists, or the replacement interface. The old clear-then-rebuild proposal remains on record as a past option, and its potential to produce tidy output should not change the criteria for judging append.

The two cards appeared later than the early records, so the old versions did not cite them. They are now attached to this history so that readers reviewing the earlier situation can separately reach the unconfirmed point in reference validation and the append-output reproduction issue, not so that the cards can serve as proof of a common cause.

The states visible in the card actions are listed below. Only the recorded transition names are retained; the available material contains no action moving XCP-223 into review.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "To Do" as Todo
  state "In Progress" as Progress
  state "In Review" as Review
  [*] --> Todo
  Todo --> Progress
  Progress --> Review
```

The compatibility cost of reference checks still lies in failure timing. If checks are delayed, existing object state may already have been used by subsequent steps, and the anomaly may appear far from the write operation; if checks are brought forward, old code may fail at the write point for the first time. Favoring checks close to the input here does not erase the latter cost. Leaving unverified keys in their original state is an indispensable part of this compromise.

The compatibility cost of append is also not just about whether the output is consistent. Retaining the old list lets reviewers see whether existing items remain, but also leaves questions of ordering and duplicates for later; rebuilding the list may appear to make output easier to control, but loses the opportunity to distinguish old items from new ones. The choice to retain the list here is intended to make it possible to judge the append operation itself, not to promise any particular formatting result.

Two points remain unresolved. First, whether the unconfirmed point identified by XCP-206 occurs during reference writing, subsequent traversal, or around relative-path saving; second, whether the instability in XCP-223 occurs only when the existing list is nonempty. The old investigation tried to use an anomaly on one side to fill a gap on the other; later records no longer take that approach.

This material continues to be cited because it preserves a boundary decision that has already been made: Keyed reference validation is discussed in terms of which objects are allowed at write time, while Skipped-test append is discussed in terms of the existing list and the results of adding new items. It also retains the early judgment that placed the two issues too close together, reminding later readers not to infer a shared root cause solely from a common regression window, similar filenames, or card titles placed side by side.

# watchOS target inference decision record

The compat-2016.4's watchOS target inference is first recorded as a boundary issue, rather than initially being reduced to a fixed rule for a particular field. The earlier investigation traced from the problem name and call name to `lib/xcodeproj/project/object/native_target.rb`; this makes that file the starting point for review, but is still insufficient to show that platform determination, build configuration, and call location already have a definite order.

Three approaches were compared at the time.

- Use a working call as the baseline and directly fill in the local inference.
- Fix the platform classification to native target, then have other objects fill in the details.
- Retain the inference location first, find a target sample that can overturn the current judgment, and decide the rule afterward.

Choose the third option. The first two have not been proven wrong; rather, a successful sample by itself cannot show whether it covers configuration differences, default values, or other construction paths. If the conditions from one passing case are written as a rule first, then different results later can only lead to more exceptions being added.

The initial working hypothesis is narrow: the classification of watchOS should be explainable within the object relationships obtained from the native target; if explaining a sample requires bypassing these relationships, that sample should be retained as a counterexample rather than used to expand the hypothesis.

This decision covers only target inference. Although Swift upgrade defaults are adjacent work in compat-2016.4, they concern the defaults used when a project is created and should remain in DOC-22. This also does not designate any one of the deployment version, SDKROOT, or platform name as the sole source in advance.

Two kinds of material have still not been obtained: the target and configuration objects reached by the successful and failed calls, respectively; and which differences between the two actually enter the inference path. Without both, inference cannot be written as a general rule.

versions.body:
# watchOS target Inference Decision Record

What the first version left behind was not a platform rule, but a narrowed decision: until there is a counterexample, do not make a single successful call bear the full explanation for every watchOS target. After that, XCP-211 kept the results of one successful call and one failed call side by side, and the record entered a different state. It can now be confirmed that there is a set of calls that must be explained together; this still does not justify claiming that we know the internal inference formula, or that a particular configuration value is the only branching factor.

This update retains the first version's cautious scope while making the review subject explicit. An implementation already exists on a branch, so the card has moved into review. This only means that concrete changes are available for review; it does not mean the rule has been accepted, much less that the failed call has a single attribution. The decision is not to skip checking the paired results on the grounds that the branch already exists.

## Scope decided now

The current decision is as follows: the existing branch must be reviewed against the successful-call and failed-call result pair; `lib/xcodeproj/project/object/native_target.rb` is the file where re-review begins; only when the difference between the two sides can be explained by the target, configuration, and read relationships actually traversed may watchOS target inference be written as a stable rule.

This does not require building a complete platform model first. This item, compat-2016.4, only needs to answer a smaller question: do the existing changes explain why this pair of calls diverged, and can that explanation be limited to the object relationships it actually covers? If the only answer is "one side looks like watchOS," the rule still cannot be finalized.

The decision also defines a stopping point. If the divergence between the successful and failed calls cannot be explained by the existing object relationships, do not label the failed call as atypical input, and do not flatten it by adding extra default values. In that case, leave the unmatched steps in place and continue treating them as part of the inference boundary. This is not delaying implementation; it is avoiding rewriting an accidentally successful path as the default semantics for every target.

## Why the first version did not take the shortest path

The first version faced a very common temptation: since a particular target had already produced the expected result, pick a name, configuration, or platform identifier associated with that call and use it as the explanation. This approach is quick to write and easy to present as a concise rule during review; the problem was that there was no evidence at the time that the call represented other targets.

Old search records included words such as platform, target, native, configurations, sdkroot, platform_name, deployment, and value. These words are useful for directing people toward code that may be relevant, but they cannot be treated as interchangeable evidence of causality. The appearance of SDKROOT in a project's text does not mean that the current inference reads it; a deployment setting matching the platform does not mean that it participates in target classification; and an object being called a native target, even less, does not mean that all platform information is generated within that object.

Therefore, the first version rejected the approach of "checking only one field." The reason for rejecting it was not that these objects had no value, but that their read timing, precedence relationships, and paths when missing had not yet been confirmed. Hard-coding any one of these would turn subsequent reviews into searches for support for a preset conclusion, rather than explanations of the different results that had already appeared.

The second approach that was abandoned was determining implementation ownership directly from the file location. The old investigation records pointed to `native_target.rb`, so that file had to be opened; but the directory location could provide only a starting point. The native target might obtain its value from the build configuration, the call site might determine when platform information is requested, and adjacent objects might handle subsequent conversion. The existing records retain this file as an entry point for review, without elevating it to a claim about all inference behavior.

The third approach that was abandoned was to call a successful call a "baseline" first, and then treat failed calls as exceptions handled separately later. In retrospect, this wording would exclude the objects requiring explanation from the rules in advance. The failure result has already been recorded, so any general judgment must be able to explain why it does not follow the same path as the successful result; when that cannot be explained, the rule should be narrowed rather than labeling the failure side as an exception.

## Changes from paired results

The local description of XCP-211 requires separately recording the results of watchOS target inference in one successful call and one failed call. It does not provide the internal decision expression, nor does it state which input property determines the platform. What it provides is a simpler and more useful constraint: the successful path can no longer be treated as an unconditional representative, and the failed path cannot be ignored.

Each result alone supports only limited judgments. The successful call shows at least that one set of inputs can reach the expected result. The failed call shows at least that these conditions do not cover all the situations currently observed. Placing them together requires the review to compare the relationships between objects; separating them makes it easy to interpret them respectively as an isolated success and an unexplained failure.

"Paired" here does not assume that all inputs to the two calls are exactly the same. They may already differ in target form, configuration contents, request timing, or other conditions not listed here. What determines the requirement is not manually turning them into exactly identical experimental inputs, but finding out where these differences begin to affect the current inference. If the two sides did not pass through the same category of target at all, the review should explicitly state that the divergence already existed before the object boundary; only if both passed through the same entry point is it necessary to continue examining configuration and platform information.

The card later added counterexamples and moved from to-do into review. The reason for the transition was that the implementation had been completed in the existing branch, so it proceeded directly to review. This historical action changed the order of work: the first version primarily waited for material that could overturn the hypothesis; now that paired results and an inspectable implementation are available, the focus has shifted to verifying whether the changes actually address the divergence. It did not overturn the first version's judgment; it only moved the stopping point for "look for counterexamples first" earlier.

## Review criteria for the divergence

The review starts from the native target entry point. What needs to be confirmed here is not whether a platform-related term appears in the filename, but which target relationship the successful and failed calls enter, respectively. If one side has already taken a different construction path before entering this object, comparing the subsequent configuration cannot by itself explain the entire difference; if both sides reach objects of the same type, the difference is more likely to lie in the configuration held by the object, the read order, or a subsequent branch.

Next, examine the relationship between the build configuration and the target. The question is not "Does the project contain configuration?" but when the native target obtains it during the current call, whether both sides obtain the same set of configuration, and which values are actually read. Even if a setting exists, it should not be listed as a cause merely because its name appears reasonable. Conversely, if a value exists on only one side, it is still necessary to confirm whether it enters the inference, rather than directly equating a textual difference with a behavioral difference.

Candidate sources of platform information are handled according to the same rules. SDKROOT, the platform name, and the deployment version can serve as directions for investigation, but this page does not presuppose their priority. If the review finds that the implementation reads one of these values, it should correlate that read with the paired results: did both the successful and failed sides reach this read; did a missing or different value change the control path; and does the change remain after the modification? If the implementation does not read a particular value at all, it should not enter this attribution merely because it exists in the project files.

Only then return to the results themselves. An acceptable explanation should connect the object relationships above with the different results of the two calls. This does not require writing a complete tour of every internal object, nor proving that all platforms use the same mechanism. It requires specifying why the change covers this current pair of calls, where that coverage stops, and ensuring that a target lacking candidate information is not quietly assigned to some unexplained default branch.

Review comments that can only confirm "the code changed" or "the successful side still works" are insufficient to change the status of this record. The existing branch is an inspectable implementation, not the basis for the decision itself. Conversely, if the review can identify the object relationship at which the two calls begin to diverge and explain how the change handles that point of divergence, the rule can be made narrower and brought closer to reality, without reserving a broad commitment for targets not involved here.

## Adjacent topics excluded from this decision

watchOS target inference often appears alongside build settings, deployment versions, and project defaults, so several boundaries need to be preserved. These are not incidental disclaimers, but safeguards against reviewers lumping different issues into a single "compatibility fix".

First, this page does not determine the rules for reading or writing the watchOS deployment version. `WATCHOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` is a deployment version setting in the build configuration; even if a sample includes this setting, the existing material does not establish it as the sole source for inference. If later findings show that it is indeed at the point of divergence, that relationship should be documented in the review notes, rather than working backward from the field name to a conclusion.

Second, this page does not address tvOS targets. The SDKROOT identifiers, deployment settings, and target classifications used by tvOS do not inherit the decisions for watchOS merely because their names are similar. compat-2016.4 contains multiple platform compatibility efforts; a pair of watchOS calls cannot establish the classification rules for another platform.

Third, Swift upgrade defaults continue to be handled by DOC-22. The upgrade-check defaults in the project root object and target platform inference belong to different object levels. The fact that both were discussed in the same round of compatibility finalization does not mean that one change can serve as an explanation for the other. When reviewers find a change in defaults, they should first distinguish whether it affects project creation or the platform classification of the current target.

Finally, this page is not a complete set of code-reading notes for `native_target.rb`. Declarations, methods, and callers in that file that are unrelated to this divergence do not need to be copied here for the sake of "coverage". Only relationships that help explain where success and failure begin to differ are material for this decision.

## Currently Acceptable and Unacceptable Conclusions

Acceptable conclusions should remain local in scope. For example, if a review shows that a particular target form reaches an explicit platform determination after obtaining a certain type of configuration, and that the difference between success and failure occurs precisely in this relationship, the rule can be limited to this form and this relationship. Such wording acknowledges its scope without including construction methods that have not yet been examined.

A conclusion that "the boundary has not yet been determined" is also acceptable. If a difference exists between the two sides, but there is no way to prove where it enters inference, the most accurate record at present is to preserve the difference and the unconfirmed connection point. In this case, a candidate field should not be selected just to make the decision look complete. The purpose of the decision is to prevent premature generalization, not to require every review to produce a fixed answer.

It is unacceptable to rewrite a failing call as an unrelated exception without explaining why it falls outside the scope of the rule. If the input objects differ, the scope may differ; but the source of the difference must be identified. Simply saying "this target is special" does not establish a boundary, because it does not tell later readers whether that specialness comes from construction, configuration, reading, or some other relationship.

It is equally unacceptable to write "the implementation is already on the branch" as "the behavior has been confirmed." Changes in the branch may be correct, or they may only allow known successful calls to continue passing. The current material provides no conclusion about merging, release, or regression, so this record does not infer those outcomes from the review request. What is retained here is the review condition, not the release status.

Another approach that looks conservative but actually loses information is to list all candidate factors together without explaining their relationship to the two calls. When SDKROOT, the platform name, configuration, and deployment settings are listed as a checklist, readers cannot tell which value actually entered the path; instead, they may mistakenly assume that these factors jointly form a confirmed rule. This item requires an explanation of the relationship, not a collection of field names.

## How to read the status

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Single sample
  Single sample --> Waiting for counterexample
  Waiting for counterexample --> Paired results retained
  Paired results retained --> Branch under review
  Branch under review --> Boundary explainable
  Branch under review --> Paired results retained: Fork not attributable
```

"Boundary explainable" is not an automatic merge status. It only means that the review can explain the success and failure by placing each back in the context of the actual object relationships. As long as either result still depends on guesswork, the status should return to "Paired results retained," continuing to preserve this pair of materials rather than ending the record with a general compatibility description.

"Branch under review" likewise does not mean that the inferred rule is finally stable. It corresponds to the fact that the card has moved from to-do into review: the implementation exists, and review has not replaced explanation. If a new form of target appears later, first determine whether it falls within the relationship already explained; it cannot automatically be treated as covered by the current decision merely because its name also contains watchOS.

## Revision to the initial wording

The direction in the initial version—"find the counterexample first, then decide where to place the rule"—remains valid, but its temporal context has passed. The counterexample has now been added, so the issue is no longer whether a failing call exists, but whether the current branch can explain its relationship to the successful call. Therefore, the waiting action in the initial version should be updated to a review action.

The initial version did not assign `native_target.rb` to a sole owner, and that remains unchanged. Even if a subsequent review finds that the actual branching point lies in an adjacent object, this does not invalidate the initial version; it only requires the review record to fill in the actual relationship from the native target entry point to that point. Conversely, without such a relationship, the adjacent object cannot be written up as the confirmed cause.

The initial version also specifically excluded Swift upgrade defaults. This boundary has not changed. When adjacent topics appear in the same compatibility cycle, it is easy to combine changes at two different levels into a single explanation; now that paired calls are available, it is even more important to avoid using project defaults to draw a conclusion in place of target inference.

What needs correcting is how the state of the material in the first version was described. At that point, there were only working hypotheses and counterexamples yet to be found; now, results from both successful and failed calls have been retained, and there is an implementation branch awaiting review. The record should no longer read as purely investigative notes. It is now a decision with an explicit review gate: the rule can move forward, but only if the object relationships are explained.

## Local questions still to be answered in review

Do the successful and failed calls encounter the same kind of native target construction? If not, at which object boundary do they begin to differ? This question determines whether the paired results compare the same branch or two paths that diverged earlier.

Do both sides obtain the build configuration at the same point? If the timing differs, does the current change depend on one of those points? There is no need to assume that the configuration necessarily determines the platform, but we must avoid mistaking "the same project text contains configuration for both" for "both read the configuration during inference."

Among SDKROOT, platform names, and deployment settings, which values actually feed into the current determination, and which merely coexist in the project? If a value is read, is it missing or different on the failed side, or is the point where it is read never reached? These distinctions determine whether the rule can be expressed as a condition rather than an after-the-fact label.

After the change, where will a target with no candidate platform information go? This item does not require new behavior to be defined for every combination of missing information, but an unexplained default must not replace the original branching. If that path cannot yet be explained, it should explicitly remain unresolved.

If review confirms that the inference point is not in the entry file, how much detail needs to be added about the relationship between the entry file and the actual inference point? At a minimum, the next review must be able to start from `native_target.rb`, find that point, and understand why this edge is relevant to the paired results; there is no need to expand the entire object graph.

Of these questions, the first two address object boundaries, the third addresses whether candidate information actually participates, the fourth prevents defaults from concealing unknowns, and the fifth addresses continuity of navigation. Together, they support the current decision, but they do not constitute an overall specification for all platform behavior.

## Decision text

For watchOS target inference in compat-2016.4, continue to use paired calls rather than a single successful sample as the basis for review. Start the review from `lib/xcodeproj/project/object/native_target.rb`; the review must explain where success and failure diverge in terms of the target, configuration, and actual read relationships. Where this can be explained, the rule should be limited to the object relationships that have been explained; where it cannot, retain the unresolved boundaries rather than substituting path location, candidate fields, or existing branches for an explanation.

The decision on this page ends here. Deployment versions, tvOS classification, project-level Swift upgrade defaults, and other code reading related to native targets are not incorporated into this inference conclusion merely because they are adjacent to this item.

# Swift Upgrade Defaults Proposal

The review of compat-2016.4 starts with `lib/xcodeproj/project.rb`. This includes `Project`, `initialize`, `self.open`, and `to_s`, and is also the entry point most likely to be discussed together when creating a new project and opening an existing one. There still isn't enough material to describe Swift upgrade defaults as established public behavior.

Start with a narrow-scope trial: observe default-value generation only in project-initialization paths, without changing file opening, serialization, or callers in the same change. Run initial processing and reprocessing consecutively on the same input, and record whether the outputs and diagnostics are stable; if the two results differ, retain the existing explicit settings and don't push the defaults into the interface layer.

There are two candidates. First, put the defaults in the `Project` new-project flow. This requires fewer caller changes, but the boundary for reopening existing projects needs to be confirmed separately. Second, have callers pass them explicitly. The behavior is easier to distinguish, but the migration surface is larger. The current preference is a narrow trial of the first option; this does not mean accepting all Swift upgrade scenarios.

Rollback conditions: repeated processing produces different results, or the original settings of an existing project are overwritten. On rollback, remove the new default selection and retain the existing explicit path. Still undecided are the specific set of defaults, how reprocessing is determined, and which callers need to migrate.

# Swift Upgrade Defaults Proposal

### Initial findings

The initial discussion considered Swift upgrade defaults alongside `lib/xcodeproj/project.rb`. The entry points in this file are straightforward: `class Project` is at line 42, `def initialize(path, skip_initialization = false)` at line 58, `def self.open(path)` at line 88, and `def to_s` at line 129. The file handles several operations for creating, opening, and writing out projects, so it was easy at first to treat "where defaults should be generated" and "how the project file is ultimately written" as the same question.

v1 limited the proposal to the initialization path to avoid rewriting existing projects as a side effect. That restriction remains. After an additional review in v2, we can still confirm only the local relationships between these entry points. The available material does not settle the full set of defaults, whether they are recalculated when an existing project is reopened, or whether callers already depend on the old behavior. Declarations along these paths are not interface commitments.

### Three options under consideration

**Put defaults in the new-project flow.** When a project is created, `Project` generates a set of default settings, so callers do not have to pass values repeatedly for each Swift upgrade scenario. This keeps the change localized and makes it easy to restrict the trial to paths related to `initialize`. The risk is that callers receive an already-constructed project object. If opening an existing project reaches the same logic, the defaults may compete with settings already in the file. This option can therefore cover only "new project" inputs initially; `open` cannot also be treated as verified.

**Put defaults in the caller.** Callers explicitly pass upgrade defaults, and `Project` only receives and saves them. The boundary is clearer, and reading an existing project is less likely to trigger the defaults accidentally. But the migration would extend outward to callers, and old call sites that omit the values would behave differently. There is no caller inventory, so we cannot assume this cost is small.

**Keep settings explicit.** This is the most conservative fallback: it introduces no new defaults and does not change the responsibilities of the existing entry points. The cost is that the upgrade experience for compat-2016.4 stays unchanged, with repeated settings still handled in multiple places. This is suitable as a temporary fallback while review results remain unstable, not as a completed upgrade solution.

This round still favors the first option, but approves only a narrow, reversible trial: defaults are applied only during initialization of a new project, and the path for opening existing files must not share this decision logic yet. "Defaults" is still just the name of the proposal, not an agreed list of fields.

### Review procedure

Review two passes over the same input. On the first pass, record the contents received by the project object and the diagnostics. On the second pass, process the same input again. Compare the actual output for stability and check for new diagnostics. Stable results on both passes mean only that this input can remain under observation; they do not establish coverage for all Swift upgrade scenarios. If the two results differ, first retain the original artifacts showing the differences, stop expanding the scope, and return to the boundary between `initialize` and `self.open` to find which step changed the object state.

Include a separate set of existing-project inputs as well. Its purpose is not to prove that the new defaults work, but to confirm that the new-project flow does not overwrite the original settings. Stop the trial at this point if original settings are replaced, repeated processing changes the output, or diagnostics appear only on the second pass. There is no specific failing output to cite, nor enough evidence to say that any caller has already been affected. Neither gap can be filled with speculation.

### Migration and rollback

If the narrow trial passes, migrate only callers that explicitly use the new-project entry point, and retain the explicit path for callers that do not need upgrade defaults. For each additional input type, repeat the comparison between the first and second passes. Stability for new projects is not grounds for including existing projects, other calling entry points, or unlisted Swift versions.

If rollback is needed, remove the added default selection and restore the callers' original explicit settings. Do not change the format of project output or existing-file reads as part of the rollback. If the issue occurs only with existing projects, roll back the shared logic and keep defaults in the new-project branch pending another check. If the issue occurs on the second pass for a new project, pause the entire trial and retain the existing behavior.

### Open decisions

- The specific fields and values for Swift upgrade defaults are undecided.
- It has not yet been confirmed whether project creation and opening in `Project` share initialization logic.
- There is no inventory of callers that need migration.
- Whether the review needs to cover more inputs depends on the first-round results; this proposal does not decide that in advance.

This is therefore not a full interface change. The only actionable decision is to start with the new-project path, process the same input twice, and record output and diagnostics. Stop and return to explicit settings if results differ or original settings are overwritten.

# Mutable scheme troubleshooting tree

The symptom is that after changing the build action, the generated scheme doesn't match the expected result. The initial observations were inconsistent: sometimes the action was still there; sometimes it was only after reopening the generated file that we found the target entry hadn't been updated. Don't classify this as a writer issue yet.

First, save the scheme from this generation and record the version used. Don't compare it directly against an older file in the working directory; first confirm that it actually came from this invocation. Then follow these two branches:

```text
Generated file is missing the expected action
├─ First check whether this entry point still receives the target entry
└─ Target entry exists but the file has no action: check build action assembly around scheme.rb

Generated file has the action, but its contents are wrong
├─ Compare against the target entry associated with the action
└─ Then check whether the difference only appears after reopening the file
```

The earlier assessment was that Mutable scheme build itself probably only takes effect on initial generation, and later changes don't make it into an existing scheme. The evidence isn't conclusive yet, so don't change the caller based on that assessment.

If the same input produces different files across versions, stop at the version difference first. The missing details are: which entry point created the action, when it was written to the file, and whether an existing scheme was involved in this generation.

# Mutable scheme troubleshooting tree

This old record still starts with "the generated scheme does not seem to include the build action just modified." It is often used to handle regressions during the compatibility period, but do not interpret the presence or absence of an action in a file as direct evidence that a particular object has stopped working. The earliest troubleshooting reduced the problem to the distinction between "initial generation" and "subsequent changes," with a very narrow starting point and overly broad conclusions.

The working hypothesis from the old record is retained as follows: Mutable scheme build is evaluated only when a new scheme is created, and existing files no longer reflect subsequent changes. This statement once conveniently explained a set of visible differences; during later review, it was insufficient to distinguish between a call still retaining an old action, the generation process not using that action, and the files being compared actually coming from different versions. Do not delete this old conclusion. When similar symptoms occur, first treat it as a hypothesis to be verified, not as a basis for recovery.

The current starting point is XCP-213. The local observation in the card is that existing calls retain Mutable scheme build; the review action is to rerun the corresponding entry point on a platform supported by the maintainers and check the actual generated file and version. Here, "version" is part of the comparison conditions, not a note appended to the end of the result. Without pairing the generated artifact with its version, the tree below can only help narrow down the location, not establish a cause.

```text
A build action anomaly is observed
│
├─ No newly generated scheme file
│  ├─ Stop at the entry point: first obtain the file and version for this entry point run
│  └─ Do not substitute an old scheme in the directory for this run's output
│
├─ The generated file exists, but the expected action is missing
│  ├─ Compare against the Mutable scheme build retained by this call
│  ├─ Compare against the target entries visible in the file
│  └─ If the two cannot be matched, check the code near the build action in lib/xcodeproj/scheme.rb
│
├─ The file contains an action, but the target associated with the action is wrong
│  ├─ First hold the input and version constant
│  ├─ Generate again through the same entry point
│  └─ Continue checking the assembly order only if the two new outputs still differ
│
└─ The file's behavior changes only when the version changes
   ├─ Record the generated file for each of the two versions
   └─ Stop calling it a single mutable-action failure
```

## What to retain first

When an issue is reported, retain at least three things: the scheme generated in this run, the version used to generate it, and the entry point that triggered generation. The old troubleshooting habit was to extract only a small action section from XML; that made it possible to see that something was "missing," but not which generation run the section came from. There is no requirement to explain the entire call chain first. Start by making the comparison objects pairable.

"The versions are the same" cannot rely solely on verbal confirmation either. What needs to be checked here is whether the version used for generation and the file at hand belong to the same review run. If the file was later retrieved from elsewhere, or was saved again after being opened, remove it from this run's sample set. It can serve as a clue, but cannot be mixed with new output to prove that an action was discarded.

If the symptom occurs only in an existing scheme, still do not immediately accept the old conclusion. Examine the existing file and this run's output separately: the former shows the result on disk at that time, while the latter shows what the entry point produced under the current conditions. Differences between them are useful, but do not automatically establish which side represents the correct state. The old record treated "existing files" as a single branch; they are now treated as separate comparison objects.

## When an action is missing

First check whether the issue description says "the action was not generated" or "the action is unavailable." These two statements were often mixed together in old tickets. The former can only be confirmed through the actual generated file; the latter also requires knowing which target entry the action corresponds to in the file. Without a file, do not conclude from the call name that the action definitely was not written out.

If this call still retains Mutable scheme build, but the generated file lacks the expected action, first focus on the local connection between the two. The source navigation entry point is `lib/xcodeproj/scheme.rb`. When examining this location, the goal is not to reread the entire scheme module, but to confirm whether the build action assembly location is actually on the path taken by this run's output. If the current entry point cannot be linked to that location, stop at "the connection has not yet been confirmed"; do not substitute the old record's statement that "the issue name once pointed here" for this step.

When the file lacks an action but the target entry is still visible, do not create a replacement action as a recovery measure either. That would overwrite the original difference. Retain the original output and rerun the same entry point once. Only if the second output still lacks the action is it worth describing the issue as a reproducible generation difference; if the second output differs, first return to the branches concerning the input, version, or whether an existing file was mixed in.

The old approach was to regenerate directly and treat the new file as the recovery result. After review, this step may only be used to locate the issue. It may produce a file that appears normal without answering why the old file lacked the action; it may also disguise a version difference as "regeneration fixed it." Therefore, retain the corresponding files both before and after the rerun, and do not overwrite the earlier file with the one left at the end.

## When the action exists but the target is wrong

This branch is more prone to misdiagnosis than "no action at all." The presence of a build action in the file does not mean that the action corresponds to the target intended for inspection in this run. Start by comparing the visible target entries in the generated file, then examine the Mutable scheme build retained by this entry point. If the two sides match, the issue may lie in the comparison objects or versions; only if they differ should you continue checking the assembly location.

Do not expand the scope to all scheme actions at this stage. This section addresses the mutability boundary of the build action. If entries related to running, testing, analysis, or archiving happen to differ as well, record them only as concurrent symptoms, and do not combine them into a single causal attribution. The old record stated in a margin note that "all actions in a scheme are unreliable"; that was an overextension and no longer applies.

If rerunning through the same entry point produces two different files, first check the versions being compared. Only when the versions and inputs match but the results still differ should this be retained as an anomaly requiring further investigation. If the versions differ, record the symptom as a version-related output change. The stopping condition here is important: without paired versions, do not proceed to assign responsibility to the writer, target, or action order.

## When old files are included in the comparison

A common misconception during the compatibility period is to treat an existing scheme on disk as the entry point's only input. It may simply be the result left by an earlier generation run, or it may have been saved again by another operation afterward. The old record did not separate this layer, causing "the change did not take effect" and "two generations of files are being compared" to end up in the same description.

When handling an existing file, first ask what role it plays in this issue: is it historical output to be observed, or an object explicitly used by this entry point? The former is only for comparison; only for the latter should you continue examining its relationship with this run's generation. If the issue description cannot answer this, retain the file but do not include it in the conclusion. Regeneration cannot supply the provenance missing from a historical file.

When "the difference was only seen after opening" occurs, return to the file itself first as well. Record the respective versions and files before and after opening, rather than directly asserting that the save process rewrote the action. The old record assigned this type of symptom to the same mutable branch; it is now listed only as a comparison condition that needs to be isolated. Without two clearly identified files, it is impossible to determine whether the change occurred during generation, reading, or subsequent saving.

## Platforms and versions

XCP-213 requires rerunning the corresponding entry point on a platform supported by the maintainers. This is not a requirement to enumerate all platforms, but a way to avoid incorrectly recording environmental differences in an unsupported environment as scheme behavior. When the platform condition is not met, collected files may be retained, but do not use them to refute the observation that existing calls still retain Mutable scheme build.

When versions change, retain at least one output from each version. Do not manually combine file contents into a "representative result," and do not record only which file looks correct. For this old entry point, the file, version, and entry point must be compared together. Until the version differences have been narrowed down, two types of action are prohibited: modifying the calling side to accommodate an old file, and changing code near `scheme.rb` to make a single sample appear consistent.

If rerun results are stable within the same version but behavior differs across versions, troubleshooting may stop at the compatibility boundary. At that point, this page can provide a starting point for further verification, but does not decide which version should become the baseline. The old record's recommendation to "simply replace the old file with the latest file" is outdated because it skips the version conditions and the observation about existing calls.

## Locations to check

On the source side, start at `lib/xcodeproj/scheme.rb`. This is a suitable location for confirming the local assembly of the build action in the scheme object and the adjacent output code; it does not replace checking the actual generated file. Start with the paired file and version, then examine the relationship between the target entry and action in the output. Working in reverse and guessing file contents solely from source code can easily carry experience from an old version into the current sample.

The facts on the calling side are currently limited to what is recorded in XCP-213: existing calls retain Mutable scheme build. This is enough to prevent the hasty conclusion that "the call has been completely removed," but not enough to prove that every generation run necessarily writes out the same set of actions. If further investigation of the connection between the call and output is needed, narrow the issue to a specific entry point run, a specific generated file, and a version. Do not make the entire compatibility layer the subject of troubleshooting.

After the interface review and risk review, the retained changes are to turn "rerunning" from a recovery method into a comparison action, and to list the version as a stopping condition. No new conclusion states that any individual branch has been fixed. When continuing to reference this record, prioritize this boundary rather than carrying forward the original initial-generation hypothesis.

## Brief handoff notes

A handoff description should state only the following clearly: whether the symptom is a missing action, an incorrect target, or version-related; whether this entry point still retains Mutable scheme build; whether the generated file and version have been paired; and whether the location near the build action in `lib/xcodeproj/scheme.rb` has been checked. Do not state the unverified "initial-generation limitation" as an established cause.

If the generated file or version is missing from the four items above, stop at insufficient samples. If all four items are present but the relationship between the target entry and action still cannot be matched, retain the original file and continue verifying from the source entry point. If differences occur only across versions, register this as a compatibility boundary; do not replace the baseline in this old troubleshooting record.
